question.text: A conservative investor who already has a well-diversified equity portfolio is looking to add one more equity fund. Fund P has a Sharpe ratio of 0.85 and Fund Q has a Sharpe ratio of 0.72. However, Fund Q has a lower correlation with the investor's existing portfolio. Which fund should the investor consider and why?

answer.text: Fund P, because it has a higher Sharpe ratio which is always the deciding factor
Fund Q, because its lower correlation with the existing portfolio may provide better diversification benefits
Neither, because the investor should not add more equity funds
Both, because they complement each other perfectly

explanation.text: The Logic: When adding a fund to an existing portfolio, what matters is not just the fund's standalone risk-adjusted return but how it interacts with the holdings already owned. A fund whose returns are less correlated with the current portfolio contributes more diversification - it can lower overall portfolio volatility relative to its return contribution. Fund Q has a slightly lower Sharpe ratio than Fund P but a lower correlation with the existing portfolio, so its addition is more likely to improve the overall portfolio's risk-return profile than Fund P, even though P looks better in isolation. The Trap: Option A treats the Sharpe ratio as the only criterion, but Sharpe is a standalone measure that ignores portfolio context. Option C unnecessarily blocks the investor from adding any equity fund. Option D ignores the fact that two funds need to be compared on their marginal contribution, not just held together. Note: The cited workbook pages (273, 274, 281, 293, 294 of the NISM Series V-A Mutual Fund Distributors workbook) discuss Sharpe ratio and the general principle of diversification, but they do not specifically discuss correlation with an existing portfolio or marginal portfolio-construction benefits. The framing above reflects general investment-management practice and standard portfolio-theory principles around diversification and correlation.
